Jaya: can you come with me to the tailor after school? need to pick up my lehenga for Saturday
Sharmila: fiiiiine
Jaya: that is a very long i 😅
Jaya: real question. is it a bored fine, a busy fine or a "Jaya you ALWAYS do this" fine?
Sharmila: lol
Sharmila: bit of all three tbh. chemistry test tomorrow and last time the tailor took an hour
Jaya: ok that's fair. what if I call first and check it's ready?
Sharmila: that would actually help
Jaya: and if it's not ready we skip it and get chai instead
Sharmila: now THAT is a proper fine 😊
Jaya: calling now
Jaya: ready. he says ten minutes max, promise
Sharmila: fine. normal-length fine. see you at the gate

qa.q: What test does Sharmila have tomorrow?
qa.a: Sharmila has a chemistry test tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling behind the long "fiiiiine"?
qa.a: Most likely Sharmila felt reluctant and a bit stressed, worried about the chemistry test and another hour at the tailor. It could also have been playful boredom rather than real annoyance, which is why Jaya asked.

qa.q: What small step turned the grudging yes into a real one?
qa.a: Jaya named the stretched word lightly, asked which kind of fine it was, and then called the tailor first so the trip would be short.

qa.q: How might the afternoon have gone if Jaya had taken the word at face value?
qa.a: Jaya would have heard a plain yes and missed the worry about the test, and Sharmila might have gone along feeling resentful.

grounding: It shows a stretched-out 'fine' in a chat carrying reluctance under a yes, with Jaya reading both the word and its rhythm before checking gently.

passage: Elizabeth's first run-through of the model-UN speech lasted fifty seconds. It was meant to take two minutes. Payal, sitting cross-legged on the bed in their Bandra flat with a phone timer, blinked. "You swallowed half the words. I heard 'climate' and then just wind." Elizabeth laughed, but her hands were cold and her heart was thumping the way it always did before a stage. "When I'm nervous my mouth just runs." "Then give it speed bumps," Payal said. She took a pencil and circled every full stop on the printout. "At each circle, stop. Let the air out, then in, then the next line." The second run was clumsy; Elizabeth kept forgetting the circles. The third time she let each breath out slowly, and the speech stretched to one minute fifty. "Better?" Payal asked. Elizabeth nodded, surprised. "It wasn't only slower. My hands stopped shaking."

qa.q: How long did Elizabeth's first run-through last?
qa.a: It lasted fifty seconds, though it was meant to take two minutes.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's racing speech suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was most likely anxious: her hands were cold and her heart was thumping, as before a stage. Part of it may also have been wanting to get the speech over with.

qa.q: What small step helped Elizabeth slow down?
qa.a: Payal circled every full stop so Elizabeth would stop there and let the air out before the next line, and practising it three times made it stick.

qa.q: What was it like for Payal to listen to the first run?
qa.a: Payal could hardly follow it, catching only 'climate' and then wind, so Payal wanted to help Elizabeth be heard, not just finish.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose speech races with nerves practising pauses at full stops with a breath out, and finding that a steadier pace also calms her body.

passage:
Tuesday night
Sent Chandrika the audition video at 4:10. Blue ticks at 4:12. Then NOTHING. By six I had decided she thought it was terrible and was too kind to say so. By seven I had re-watched it eleven times and found every flat note. Amma said, "Ganga, beti, the phone won't answer faster if you stare at it." At dinner I nearly typed "fine, forget it" but didn't. Instead I wrote: "hey, are you busy or did you hate it? either is ok, just tell me 🙂" Honestly only half ok. Reply at 9:40: "SORRY. Tuition till 9, phone in the bag. Watched it on the bus and wanted to write something proper, not just 'nice'. The high part gave me goosebumps!!" So: five hours of spiralling for a bus ride and tuition. Note to self: ask first, panic later.

qa.q: When did Chandrika's reply arrive?
qa.a: The reply arrived at 9:40.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling while waiting for a reply?
qa.a: Ganga felt anxious and afraid of rejection, deciding by six that Chandrika thought the video was terrible and re-watching it eleven times. Some of it may also have been nerves about the audition itself.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Ganga read the silence as a verdict and spiralled for hours; a direct, low-pressure question brought the real reason, tuition and a phone in the bag. 👍

qa.q: Why might Chandrika have waited to reply?
qa.a: Chandrika was at tuition till nine and then wanted to write something proper rather than just 'nice', so the delay came from care, not rejection.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a long reply delay as rejection, spiralling, and then asking directly and learning the delay meant something else.

passage: So, for the podcast: I'm Irawati, class eleven, and my story is about a sentence I never finished. We were on Kavitha's terrace, eating roasted corn, and I was telling her about my brother moving to the hostel in Kota. I said, "And the worst part is that Amma keeps setting four plates and then—" and I just stopped. Mid-word. I stared at the water tank. Kavitha told me afterwards she had no idea what the silence meant. Was I angry with her for asking? Embarrassed? About to cry? Just thinking? Honestly, a bit of all of it. What she did was put her corn down and say, "You don't have to finish that. I'm around, whenever." Then she talked about the kite stuck on the wire. Two days later, on the school bus, I finished the sentence, and she just listened.

qa.q: What were they eating on Kavitha's terrace?
qa.a: They were eating roasted corn.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been feeling when the sentence stopped?
qa.a: Most likely a wave of sadness about the brother's empty place at the table, but by Irawati's own account it was also partly embarrassment and just thinking, so the silence was mixed.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do well?
qa.a: Kavitha did not guess or push: putting the corn down, saying Irawati didn't have to finish, and switching to the kite gave space while leaving the door open. 🤍

qa.q: How did the silence look from Kavitha's side?
qa.a: Kavitha could not tell whether it meant anger at her, embarrassment, tears or thought, so she chose a reply that would work for any of them.

grounding: It shows a teenager stopping mid-sentence, the silence being open to several readings, and a caring reply that gives space and invites talk later.

passage:
Monday. Reena had moved to the Chennai school three weeks ago and still ate lunch alone. At home she crooned old Bengali songs from Dida's cassettes under her breath while doing homework, the slow ones about rivers and leaving. Her mother, Anjali, paused at the door, listening, and wondered if Reena was miserable.
Thursday. In music period Reena hummed one of those tunes without meaning to. Two classmates leaned over. "What's that? Teach us." By the bell, three of them were mangling the Bengali words together and laughing so hard the teacher had to clap twice.
The next Monday. Reena sang loudly in the shower, the same river song, now with the lunch group's made-up harmony on the chorus. Anjali knocked and asked, "Still the sad one?" Reena opened the door with wet hair, grinning. "It's not sad any more, Ma. It's ours."

qa.q: Whose cassettes did the old Bengali songs come from?
qa.a: They came from Dida's cassettes.

qa.q: What does Reena's crooning on the first Monday suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It may show Reena felt lonely and homesick, eating lunch alone after the move and choosing songs about leaving. But it could also be comfort or pride in songs from Dida, so the lyrics alone don't prove sadness.

qa.q: How could Anjali support Reena without reading too much into the lyrics?
qa.a: Anjali could ask lightly what the songs mean to Reena, as with 'Still the sad one?', rather than deciding from the words that Reena is miserable.

qa.q: How did the song feel for the classmates who leaned over?
qa.a: For them it became something fun to learn and mangle together, a shared group tune rather than a sad one.

grounding: It shows a teenager crooning songs that first carry longing and later belonging, and a parent learning that the lyrics chosen do not prove the teen's mood.

passage: The argument with Papa had been about the scooter keys and leaving late, and it was still ringing in Hemant's ears when he reached the exam centre in Secunderabad. His jaw was tight. He pulled on his headphones, but instead of playing music he hummed an old film tune under his breath, the one Papa whistled while shaving. By the third round his shoulders dropped and he could finally read the seating chart. Devika, his cousin from the same colony, found him by the gate. "You're humming. That usually means trouble." "It helps," Hemant said. "Tell you after." After the paper, sitting on the metro steps with two cups of chai, he told her about the keys and the shouting. Devika listened, then said, "Call him before dinner. Tell him you were scared of missing the exam, not just angry." Hemant hummed one bar, then dialled.

qa.q: What had the argument with Papa been about?
qa.a: It had been about the scooter keys and leaving late.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as he hummed by the exam centre?
qa.a: Hemant was tense and still upset from the argument, shown by his tight jaw. Choosing the tune Papa whistles may also hint that he missed feeling close to Papa, not only exam nerves.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Humming settled Hemant enough to read the chart, and talking it through with Devika afterwards led to calling Papa, so the song calmed him and the talk helped repair things.

qa.q: How does Devika read Hemant's humming?
qa.a: Devika sees it as a sign that something is wrong, 'That usually means trouble', so she stays close and listens once he is ready.

grounding: It shows a teenager humming under headphones to calm down after a conflict and before an exam, alongside talking it through with a trusted person.

passage:
Thursday
Yusuf has greeted me the same way since class seven: "morning dino 🦖" on the phone, and our silly three-part handshake at the gate. Today the message said just "hi." With a full stop. A FULL STOP. At the gate he gave me a nod, like I was a teacher. Then I asked if he had the maths sheet and he didn't reply all afternoon. I spent geography building a whole story: he's found cooler friends, I said something wrong on Monday, the handshake era is over. At six I made myself write, "you ok? you went full formal on me 😅". He wrote back: "sorry Rehana, phone screen cracked, typing is pain. and my uncle was at the gate, didn't want to do dino hands in front of him lol." So. One full stop and a cracked screen. Keeping the story ideas for English class.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's message say today?
qa.a: It said just "hi." with a full stop.

qa.q: What was Rehana worried about during geography?
qa.a: Rehana felt anxious and a bit hurt, reading the full stop and the nod as distance and imagining Yusuf had found cooler friends. It may also have been plain overthinking on a quiet day.

qa.q: What would you advise Rehana next time a greeting changes?
qa.a: Check before building a story: a short, light question like the six o'clock message gets the real reason faster than an afternoon of guessing.

qa.q: What was the nod at the gate like from Yusuf's side?
qa.a: For Yusuf it was just avoiding the silly handshake in front of his uncle, not pulling away, so he probably had no idea it caused worry.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a change in a greeting and one missed reply as distance, then asking and finding it meant something else.

passage: Zeenat had one minute to convince the student council, squeezed into the Kochi school's AV room, to drop plastic cups from the annual fest. She held up a drawing: a single cup, an arrow to a drain, an arrow to the backwaters behind the school, then a fish. "Every cup we use on Friday ends up in our own canal," she said. "Remember the monsoon, when the drain by the canteen choked? I pulled cups out of it myself." Heads nodded. People remembered the smell. Then she added, "And a video says ninety percent of fish have plastic inside." Jomon, from class twelve, raised a hand. "Which video? Who measured?" Zeenat opened her mouth, then closed it. She didn't know. "I'll check that one," she said. "But the drain, you all saw." The vote passed. That night she hunted for the study and replaced the claim with one she could name.

qa.q: What did Zeenat's drawing show?
qa.a: It showed a single cup, a drain, the backwaters behind the school, and then a fish.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when Jomon asked 'Which video?'
qa.a: Zeenat was probably caught off guard and a little embarrassed, since her mouth opened and closed and she didn't know the source. She may also have felt determined, because she promised to check instead of defending it.

qa.q: Which part of Zeenat's pitch was strongest, and what needed fixing?
qa.a: The drain story worked because everyone had seen it; the fish figure from an unnamed video needed checking, and replacing it with a named source fixed that.

qa.q: How might the council have reacted later if Jomon hadn't asked?
qa.a: They might have voted on a claim nobody could trace, and trusted Zeenat's examples less if it later turned out to be wrong.

grounding: It shows a teenager using a diagram and a shared memory to persuade peers, and learning to check the source behind a vivid claim.

passage:
Anirban: Ma'am, sorry to message on the school portal. Rudra and two others are planning to climb the old gym roof after practice today to film a jump.
Kavitha Ma'am: Thank you for telling me, Anirban. Are you somewhere you can talk?
Anirban: Yes, library. Also... Rudra kicked me out of the team chat last week. So maybe you think I'm just getting back at him.
Kavitha Ma'am: I'm not deciding why you told me. What matters is that someone could get hurt. Did you see the plan yourself?
Anirban: He posted "gym roof 5pm, bring phone" before I got removed. I have a screenshot.
Kavitha Ma'am: Please send it. I'm going to Coach now, and the roof door will be locked before practice ends.
Kavitha Ma'am: The team chat thing sounds hurtful too. Want to talk about that at 4?
Anirban: ok. thank you ma'am 🙏
Kavitha Ma'am: 4:00, staffroom. See you there.

qa.q: Where was Anirban when he messaged?
qa.a: Anirban was in the library.

qa.q: What might Anirban be worried about when he mentions the team chat?
qa.a: Anirban seems worried that Kavitha Ma'am will think it's revenge, and is still hurt at being kicked out. The likeliest reading is mixed motives: real fear for safety alongside that sting.

qa.q: Which steps did Kavitha Ma'am take, and why do they work?
qa.a: She thanked Anirban, didn't judge the motive, asked for the evidence, went to Coach and had the roof door locked the same day, then offered time for the hurt.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha Ma'am had focused on Anirban's motive?
qa.a: Anirban might have felt accused and stopped talking, and the roof jump could have gone ahead while they argued about why Anirban told.

grounding: It shows a teenager reporting a peer's risky plan with possibly mixed motives, and an adult who says thank you, listens without assuming and acts on safety the same day.

passage:
Wednesday, late
Told Ira at recess that I'm leaving the quiz team. Ira put her samosa down and started: "So you're saying you're bored of quiz? Or bored of Varun being captain? Why now, two weeks before inter-school? Why didn't you tell Ma'am first?" Four questions in one breath, eyebrows up, like a TV lawyer. I felt cornered and said, "Can I finish one sentence, please?" Ira went quiet and picked at the samosa. On the walk home she tried again, slower: "I asked that badly. I'm not trying to catch you out, Damini. I'll just miss doing the rapid-fire round with you. What's actually going on?" Same kind of question, totally different feeling. So I told her the real thing: Varun laughs every time I get one wrong. She said, "So you're saying it's him, not quiz?" Yes. Exactly that.

qa.q: Where did Ira start asking the questions?
qa.a: Ira started at recess, after putting her samosa down.

qa.q: How did Damini feel when Ira fired four questions at recess?
qa.a: Damini felt cornered and irritated, snapping 'Can I finish one sentence, please?' It may also have been embarrassment about the real reason, Varun laughing.

qa.q: What made the second round of questions work better?
qa.a: Ira slowed down, admitted asking badly, gave the caring reason for asking, and asked one open question, so the probing felt like support instead of a trial.

qa.q: How might Ira have seen the first round of questions?
qa.a: Ira probably meant them as surprise and care about the timing, and was hurt when Damini snapped, going quiet and picking at the samosa.

grounding: It shows 'so you're saying' and probing questions feeling like interrogation at first and like support later, depending on tone and the reason behind them.
